answers: A hiker's fatal fall in March has been blamed on using a smartphone app map instead of an actual map. The BBC reports Jane Wilson and her husband Gary were hiking on Tryfan in Wales when it started to get dark and they decided to skip the summit. While attempting to descend the mountain, Gary was looking at an Ordnance Survey app while Jane went a short way ahead to make sure the path was safe, according to the Telegraph. The Manchester Evening News reports Gary heard his wife fall, got to safety, and called for help. Rescuers found the 53-year-old librarian's body at the bottom of a 30-foot cliff with a fractured skull. At a hearing Friday, Jane's was ruled an accidental death due, in part, to using an app instead of a map. "Apart from potential difficulties caused by poor detail on an electronic map, batteries on mobile phones have a nasty habit of running out just when you need them most," the Telegraph quotes a spokesperson for Mountain Rescue England and Wales as saying. A detective says the app map "would have been small and not as detailed" and took the couple on a route that was not the safest. A director with Ordnance Survey says hikers should always use the app in conjunction with an actual map "due to the nature of mobile devices when navigating the real world." Authorities also say Jane wasn't wearing appropriate footwear for the hike. (Go inside the futile search for "Inchworm" on the trail.)

**Summary of News Passages:**

On March 25, Jane Wilson, a 53-year-old experienced mountain walker and academic engagement librarian at the University of Manchester, tragically fell to her death while attempting to find a safe route down the west face of Tryfan in Snowdonia, Wales. She and her husband, Gary Wilson, had decided not to ascend to the summit as dusk approached and opted to descend via a different route using Mr. Wilson’s smartphone app. 

According to Mr. Wilson, Jane had gone ahead to scout a route and asked him if it was safe. He confirmed they would only proceed if both agreed. Shortly after, he heard an exclamation followed by the sound of a rock fall, realizing Jane had fallen. He climbed to a safer ledge and raised the alarm, as he feared he might also be injured if he attempted to descend. 

Members of the Ogwen Valley Mountain Rescue Team eventually located Jane’s body over 150 meters below, where she had fractured her skull and sustained other severe injuries. Detective Constable Tim Bird, leader of the rescue team, explained that Jane had fallen approximately 20-30 feet down a vertical cliff and tumbled about 150 meters into an area known as Notch arrete. He noted that although the weather was dry, Jane’s light boots were unsuitable for the rough terrain, increasing the risk of slipping. 

Bird also emphasized that the couple’s decision to traverse the west face instead of using a more established route like the North Ridge was a contributing factor. He stated that the smartphone app used by Mr. Wilson provided less detailed information than a traditional map and that the couple may have misinterpreted a footpath, leading them to an unsafe route. 

The inquest concluded Jane’s death as accidental. Despite her experience in mountain walking and scrambling, along with her participation in marathons such as the New York Marathon and Great North Run, the combination of terrain, footwear, and navigation choices led to the tragic incident. 

In response to the incident, officials from Mountain Rescue England and Wales have reiterated the importance of using traditional navigation tools like maps and compasses alongside electronic devices. They caution that electronic navigation can be unreliable due to limited detail and potential battery failure. Chris Lloyd, a member of the Ogwen Rescue team, noted that Tryfan is responsible for about 30% of the incidents the team responds to, highlighting the mountain’s inherent risks.
